subject: Social Science
title: The Economy is Everywhere: How People Produce and Trade
hook: How do villages and cities produce goods? How does food reach your plate? How does money move?

characters.name: Ananya
characters.role: A curious 12-year-old from a town in Maharashtra

characters.name: Farmer Bhagwan
characters.role: Ananya's uncle who grows sugarcane and sells it to a factory

characters.name: Mr. Patel
characters.role: A shop owner who sells goods from many local and distant producers

slides.title: Economic Activities Around Us
slides.storyContext: Ananya buys lunch at school: rice (from Punjab), curry (with vegetables from a farm near her town), chapati (wheat from Madhya Pradesh), salt (from Gujarat). In an hour, she's consumed products from 5 different regions, made by hundreds of people, bought and sold by traders. She doesn't realize it, but she's witnessing 'the economy' in action.

image.alt: Economic Activities Around Us — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: From Field to Table
slides.storyContext: Farmer Bhagwan grows sugarcane on his 5-acre farm. He sells it to a sugar factory 30 km away. The factory processes it into sugar and sells it to wholesalers in the city. The wholesalers sell to shop owners like Mr. Patel. Mr. Patel sells sugar to families like Ananya's. Along the way: the farmer earned income, the factory created jobs, traders made profit, shopkeeper provided service. The 'economy' is this entire chain of production and trade.

slides.title: A Day in Ananya's Economic Life
slides.storyContext: Ananya wakes up, eats breakfast (milk from a dairy farm, bread from a bakery, butter from a churning cooperative). Her mother buys vegetables at the market (from local farmers). Her father takes an auto-rickshaw to work (the driver earns a living). Ananya goes to school (the teacher is paid a salary). Everything she does involves dozens of people earning, trading, and serving. She is part of an economy without realizing it.

slides.title: What is an Economy? Production, Distribution, and Consumption
slides.storyContext: An economy is how a society organizes to produce what people need, distribute it fairly, and consume it without waste.

points.label: Production
points.text: Creating goods (food, clothes, tools) and services (teaching, healing, transportation). Farmers produce food; factories produce goods; teachers provide services.

points.label: Distribution
points.text: Moving goods from producers to consumers. Traders, transporters, shopkeepers, and wholesalers handle distribution. They earn profit.

points.label: Consumption
points.text: People using goods and services. A family consumes food, clothes, and healthcare. A business consumes raw materials.

points.label: Flow of money
points.text: Money moves in reverse: consumers pay shopkeepers, who pay wholesalers, who pay factories, who pay farmers. This circular flow sustains the economy.

example.problem: Trace the economy for a cotton shirt: (1) Who produces it? (2) How does it reach the shop? (3) How do different people earn?
example.solution: (1) Farmer grows cotton → mill spins thread → factory stitches shirt. (2) Factory sells to wholesaler → wholesaler to retailer → retailer to customer. (3) Farmer earns from cotton, mill worker earns wage, factory owner earns profit, retailer earns markup, transporter earns fee. Everyone in the chain benefits.

slides.inSimpleWords: An economy is the system of producing, distributing, and consuming goods. Money moves through this system, supporting everyone involved.

slides.title: Economy in Action: Tracing a Rice Grain
slides.storyContext: Ananya's rice grain started in a paddy field in Punjab. A farmer planted, watered, harvested, and threshed it. He sold to a wholesaler (profit: 500/sack). The wholesaler sold to a miller (profit: 100). The miller cleaned and packaged it, sold to a retailer (profit: 150). The retailer sold to Ananya's mother (profit: 50). The grain crossed 5 states, 6 transactions, and fed a family.

example.problem: A farmer sells rice at 500/sack. The retailer sells it at 800/sack (including costs). How much value was added by the wholesaler, miller, and retailer combined?
example.solution: 800 - 500 = 300/sack total value-add. Breaking down: wholesaler and transportation add 100, miller adds 100, retailer adds 100. Each step justified by effort, risk, and cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every product that reaches you has traveled through an economy, with each person adding value.

slides.title: Agricultural Economy: Farming and Food Production
slides.storyContext: Ananya's region is agricultural. Most people farm or work in farm-related jobs: making tools, storing grains, selling produce, processing food.

points.label: Subsistence farming
points.text: A farmer grows food mainly for his own family's consumption. No surplus to sell. Common in poorer regions.

points.label: Commercial farming
points.text: A farmer grows crops specifically for sale (sugarcane, cotton, wheat, spices). Tries to maximize yield and profit.

points.label: Cropping patterns in India
points.text: Rice and wheat (staples) in North, spices in South, cotton in Gujarat/Andhra, sugarcane in Maharashtra/Uttar Pradesh, tea in Assam/Himachal.

points.label: Agricultural support
points.text: Government helps through subsidies (cheaper seeds/fertilizer), irrigation, crop insurance, and minimum support prices (MSP).

example.problem: Farmer Bhagwan grew sugarcane but faced two problems: (1) unseasonal rain damaged 20% of the crop, (2) a factory paid less than last year. How does the government help?
example.solution: (1) Crop insurance compensates for weather damage. (2) Minimum Support Price (MSP) guarantees a floor price—if the market price drops below MSP, the government buys at MSP. This gives farmers security.

slides.inSimpleWords: Farming is a major economic activity in India. Farmers produce food and cash crops. The government helps farmers through subsidies and price support.

image.alt: Agricultural Economy: Farming and Food Production — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: Farmer Bhagwan's Seasons
slides.storyContext: Bhagwan's year: December-May is sugarcane season (planting, growing, harvesting). May-September is monsoon (uncertainty—too much rain causes disease, too little causes drought). He borrows money from a bank for seeds and fertilizer, repays after harvest. One bad season and he's in debt. Government MSP protects him, but so does diversification (he grows some wheat too).

slides.title: Understanding MSP (Minimum Support Price)
slides.storyContext: The government announces: MSP for sugarcane is 500/quintal. If the market price falls to 450, the government buys at 500. If the market price rises to 550, farmers sell at 550 (free market). MSP sets a floor, not a ceiling.

example.problem: Bhagwan produced 100 quintals. Market price dropped to 450. What would he earn without MSP vs. with MSP?
example.solution: Without MSP: 100 × 450 = 45,000. With MSP: 100 × 500 = 50,000. He saves 5,000 (security). This is why MSP matters for farmer livelihoods.

slides.inSimpleWords: MSP guarantees farmers a minimum price for their crops so they don't lose money in bad years.

slides.title: Industrial Economy: Manufacturing and Factories
slides.storyContext: Ananya visits a sugar factory near her town. She sees: sugarcane entering, machines processing, sugar bags being packaged and loaded onto trucks. The factory employs 200 workers, runs 24/7, and produces 500 tons of sugar daily.

points.label: What are industries?
points.text: Businesses that use machines and labor to transform raw materials into finished products. Cotton → fabric → clothes. Sugarcane → sugar.

points.label: Types of industries
points.text: Primary (extractive): mining, forestry. Secondary (manufacturing): textile mills, sugar factories, steel plants. Tertiary (services): transport, shops, schools.

points.label: Cottage industries
points.text: Small-scale, home-based production (pottery, weaving, handicrafts). Employ 1-5 people. Important for rural income.

points.label: Factory jobs and working conditions
points.text: Factories provide employment but workers often face low wages, long hours, and unsafe conditions. Labor laws protect workers' rights.

example.problem: A textile factory produces 1000 shirts daily. Its output over a year is 365,000 shirts. This creates jobs for 100 workers, income for cotton farmers, and profit for the owner. But a worker earns only 10,000/month. Is this fair?
example.solution: The worker should earn at least the minimum wage (varies by state, typically 8,000-12,000/month). If the factory profits are high, workers should share in the gains. Worker unions and labor laws push for fair wages.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factories use machines and workers to make goods from raw materials. They create jobs and income but must treat workers fairly.

slides.title: Inside the Sugar Factory
slides.storyContext: Ananya tours the factory with Bhagwan. Sugarcane arrives by truck, is crushed to extract juice, juice is boiled in massive vats to evaporate water, crystal sugar forms, and bags are filled. She meets Ramesh, who operates a machine for 12 hours, earns 400/day. She also meets the factory manager who oversees production, quality, and profit margins. Same factory, different roles, different pay.

slides.title: Factory Economy: From Cost to Profit
slides.storyContext: The sugar factory buys 1000 tons of sugarcane at 500/quintal (10,000 quintals = 100 lakh). Operating costs: labor (20 lakh), electricity (15 lakh), equipment (10 lakh), transport (5 lakh). Total: 150 lakh. Output: 300 tons of sugar, sold at 50/kg = 150 lakh.

example.problem: Revenue = 150 lakh, Costs = 150 lakh. No profit! What happened?
example.solution: The calculation is illustrative—real factories have better sugar yield, lower costs, or higher selling prices. But this shows why factories depend on efficiency. A 10% cost cut or 10% price rise changes loss to profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factories must manage costs carefully. Every worker, every machine, every gram of material matters to profit.

slides.title: Service Economy: Doctors, Teachers, Shops, Transportation
slides.storyContext: Services are invisible but essential. Ananya's school teacher (education), the doctor at the clinic (health), the rickshaw driver (transport), and shop owners (retail) all provide services.

points.label: What are services?
points.text: Intangible work that helps or serves people: teaching, healthcare, transportation, entertainment, banking, government. Services don't produce physical goods.

points.label: Growing importance
points.text: In developed economies, services dominate (over 70% of GDP). In India, it's 55% and growing as people get richer.

points.label: Informal services
points.text: Street vendors, auto-rickshaw drivers, domestic workers, small repair shops—these provide crucial services but are unorganized and underpaid.

points.label: Formal services
points.text: Hospitals, schools, banks, government offices—regulated, with fixed prices/fees and employee protections.

example.problem: Ananya's father uses these services in a month: doctor (500), school (5,000), bus transport (200), restaurant (1,500), barber (100). Total: 7,300 spent on services. Does services cost too much?
example.solution: Services are expensive because they require skilled people's time. A good teacher justifies their fee; a good doctor, their consultation fee. But many services (schools, buses) are subsidized by government to keep them affordable. The market price alone would exclude the poor.

slides.inSimpleWords: Services like teaching, healthcare, and transportation don't make physical goods but are crucial to society. They're a growing part of the economy.

slides.title: The Rickshaw Driver's Day
slides.storyContext: Ananya rides in an auto-rickshaw to school. The driver, Suresh, wakes at 6 AM, checks his vehicle, takes passengers all day. He earns 600/day (if he gets 8 passengers at 100-150 each, minus fuel). He has no fixed salary, no benefits, no sick leave. But his service is essential—Ananya wouldn't reach school without him.

slides.title: Comparing Formal and Informal Services
slides.storyContext: Ananya's school teacher (formal): fixed salary 30,000/month, benefits, pension, job security. Rickshaw driver (informal): 600/day, no benefits, no security, vulnerable to fuel price hikes and competition.

example.problem: Why do informal workers earn less than formal workers doing similar skilled work?
example.solution: Formal jobs have employer stability (budget), contracts, regulation. Informal workers are self-employed, variable income, no safety net. Government pushes formalization (registering informal workers, providing insurance) to improve lives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Formal jobs are stable and regulated; informal jobs are flexible but risky and often underpaid.

slides.title: Trade and Markets: How Goods Flow Between Regions
slides.storyContext: Ananya's lunch has ingredients from 5 states. Sugar from Maharashtra reaches her town through traders. A trader buys in bulk from the factory, sells to wholesalers, who sell to retailers. Each earns a markup.

points.label: Why trade?
points.text: Different regions produce different goods based on climate, soil, and resources. Trade lets people access goods from everywhere. Coffee grows in South, rice in North. Trade connects them.

points.label: Local markets
points.text: Villages and towns have weekly markets where farmers sell produce and artisans sell goods. Face-to-face trading.

points.label: Regional and national trade
points.text: Wholesale markets (mandis) aggregate goods. Traders, middlemen, and transporters move goods across states. Cities have large retail markets.

points.label: Markup and profit
points.text: Each intermediary (wholesaler, transporter, retailer) adds a markup. This is how they earn. But too many middlemen inflate prices.

example.problem: Sugarcane costs the farmer 400 per quintal. The factory pays 500 (profit: 100). The wholesaler marks up to 600 (100 profit). The retailer to 700 (100 profit). The final price to consumers is 700. Is this fair?
example.solution: It depends on services rendered. The factory processes (labor, machines). The wholesaler stores and transports (cost and risk). The retailer has a shop and serves customers. Each markup reflects their service. But if there are too many middlemen with no value-add, the final price becomes high and farmers get squeezed. The government is promoting direct-to-consumer trade (farmers selling directly in markets, cutting middlemen).

slides.inSimpleWords: Trade connects different regions. Goods flow from producers to consumers through traders and markets. Each person in the chain adds value.

image.alt: Trade and Markets: How Goods Flow Between Regions — Economic Activities Around Us

slides.title: A Day at the Mandi (Wholesale Market)
slides.storyContext: Ananya visits the agricultural mandi in her district. Hundreds of farmers arrive with produce at dawn. Middlemen (commission agents) assess quality, negotiate bulk deals, arrange transport. Wholesalers bid for goods. By 10 AM, goods are sorted, packed, and trucks leave for city retail markets. The mandi is the economic hub—controlled chaos, fortunes made and lost, farmers either satisfied or exploited.

slides.title: The Mandi Chain: From Farmer to Consumer
slides.storyContext: A farmer brings 10 tons of onions to the mandi at 15/kg = 150,000. Commission agent takes 5% (7,500). Wholesaler buys at 16/kg (160,000 - 7,500 commission to agent = 152,500 to farmer). Wholesaler sells to retailer at 18/kg. Retailer sells to consumer at 25/kg.

example.problem: Calculate profit at each step and final consumer price.
example.solution: Farmer: 150,000. Agent: 7,500. Wholesaler: 160,000 - 152,500 = 7,500 profit. Retailer: 25 × 10,000 = 250,000 - (18 × 10,000) = 70,000 profit (includes shop costs, risk). Consumer price: 25/kg. Markup seems high but each person handles risk and provides service.

slides.inSimpleWords: The mandi connects farmers to wholesale and retail markets. Each buyer adds value and takes risk.

slides.title: Money and Banking: How Transactions Work
slides.storyContext: Farmer Bhagwan sells sugarcane for 50,000 rupees. He deposits this in a bank. Later, he borrows 100,000 at 8% interest to buy fertilizer. The bank takes his deposit money from others and lends it to him. This is how money circulates in the economy.

points.label: Money's role
points.text: Money is a medium of exchange. Without it, people would barter (trade directly). Money makes transactions efficient.

points.label: Banking system
points.text: Banks accept deposits from people, pay interest, and lend to others at higher interest. The difference is their profit.

points.label: Credit and loans
points.text: Farmers borrow for seeds and fertilizer. Businesses borrow to expand. People borrow to build houses. Banks enable economic growth through lending.

points.label: Interest rates and inflation
points.text: High interest rates discourage borrowing. Low rates encourage it. The central bank (RBI in India) sets policy rates to manage the economy.

example.problem: Farmer Bhagwan borrows 100,000 at 8% interest for 1 year. How much must he repay?
example.solution: 100,000 + (100,000 x 8/100) = 100,000 + 8,000 = 108,000. If his sugarcane harvest yields 150,000 profit, he can repay easily. But if the harvest fails (weather, pest), he's in debt. This is why crop insurance exists.

slides.inSimpleWords: Banks accept money from savers and lend it to borrowers at interest. This helps businesses and individuals grow. Money circulates through the economy.

slides.title: Bhagwan's Loan
slides.storyContext: Bhagwan needs 100,000 for fertilizer and seeds. He goes to the bank with a land deed. The bank approves a loan at 8% annual interest, payable over 2 years. Monthly EMI (installment) = 4,600. If he grows good sugarcane (200 quintals at 500/quintal = 100,000), he can repay from harvest. But if prices fall or yield drops, he struggles. This is why farmers fear debt and seek government support.

slides.title: Interest and Compound Growth
slides.storyContext: Ananya's mother deposits 50,000 in a savings account at 5% annual interest. After 1 year: 50,000 + 2,500 = 52,500. After 2 years: 52,500 + 2,625 = 55,125. Money grows even if you don't work!

example.problem: How long does it take 50,000 to double at 5% interest?
example.solution: Rough estimate (Rule of 72): 72 ÷ 5 = 14.4 years. Exact: ~14.2 years. Power of compound interest—savings grow exponentially.

slides.inSimpleWords: Interest makes your money grow over time. Savings earn interest; loans cost interest. Banks are middlemen in this exchange.

slides.title: Challenge: A Complete Economic Chain
slides.storyContext: Trace the complete economic chain for a piece of clothing—from cotton production to your wardrobe. Identify: (1) All producers/workers involved, (2) All transactions and money flows, (3) All services provided.

example.problem: A cotton shirt costs 500 in a shop. Trace where this money goes. Start with: Farmer grows cotton (earns ?), Mill processes cotton (earns ?), Factory stitches shirt (earns ?), Transporter delivers (earns ?), Retailer sells (earns ?).
example.solution: One breakdown: Farmer 80, Miller 60, Factory 120, Transporter 40, Retailer markup 200 (profit after costs). Total = 500. This shows how a price is built by multiple contributors. Different markups reflect different efforts and risks.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every product involves many workers, businesses, and services. Money distributed among them is how the economy sustains millions of people.

slides.title: Challenge: Design Your Own Mandi
slides.storyContext: Imagine you're a farmer who wants to bypass middlemen and sell directly to retailers. Design a system: How would you find buyers? How would you set prices? What risks would you face?

points.label: Direct sales
points.text: Farmers' collectives are forming—cooperative groups buy from farmers at fair prices, sell to retailers, skip commission agents. Risk: organizing farmers, maintaining quality standards.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direct-to-consumer trade reduces middlemen but requires organization and coordination.

slides.title: Challenge: Economic Decision-Making
slides.storyContext: Bhagwan has 50,000 saved. He can: (A) deposit in bank at 5% (steady but slow growth), (B) invest in better seeds/fertilizer (risky but could double harvest), (C) lend to a neighbor at 10% (good return but risk of default). What should he do?

points.label: Analysis
points.text: A is safe, 2,500/year. B is risky—if harvest fails, he loses money. C is medium-risk. Most farmers choose A + B (some safe, some invested), or seek government subsidies to reduce risk of B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Economic decisions involve weighing risk, return, and security. People's choices shape the economy.

slides.title: Challenge: Spot the Economy
slides.storyContext: Look at your daily routine—sleeping, eating, going to school, playing. For each activity, list: (1) Who produced it? (2) Who transported it? (3) Who sold it? (4) Who earned money?

points.label: Example: Breakfast
points.text: Milk: Dairy farmer produced, transport company delivered, shopkeeper sold. Eggs: Farmer raised chickens, shopkeeper sold. Bread: Baker made, shopkeeper sold. All earn.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every moment of your day, the economy is working behind the scenes.

slides.title: Global Economy Connected to You
slides.storyContext: Ananya's new shoes: rubber from Malaysia, stitching in Vietnam, shipped to Mumbai, sold in her local shop. One pair of shoes involves millions of economic transactions across continents and weeks.

example.problem: A pair of shoes costs 1,500 in a shop. Estimate costs: factory labor, materials, shipping, wholesale markup, retail profit.
example.solution: Materials: 300, labor: 150, shipping: 50, factory profit: 100, wholesaler: 200, retailer: 800 profit (includes rent, staff, risk). The global supply chain is complex but the principle is same: value adds at each step.

slides.inSimpleWords: Modern economies are global—products travel far, and money flows through many countries.

slides.title: The Economy is Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Ananya now sees that every meal, every object, and every service is part of a vast economic web. Farmers, factories, traders, shopkeepers, and service providers all connect.

points.text: An economy produces, distributes, and consumes goods and services.
Agricultural economy: farming is a major sector, supported by government subsidies and MSP.
Industrial economy: factories transform raw materials into finished goods and employ workers.
Service economy: teachers, doctors, transporters, shopkeepers provide essential services.
Trade and markets connect regions. Traders, wholesalers, and retailers facilitate exchange.
Money and banking enable transactions and help businesses and people grow.

slides.inSimpleWords: The economy is everywhere—in food, clothes, schools, hospitals, shops. It works because millions of people produce, trade, and serve each other.

subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Geometry Adventure
hook: Raj discovers lines and angles hidden in his apartment building.

slides.title: Raj's Geometry Adventure
slides.storyContext: Raj looks out his window and sees the edges of buildings, the horizon line, the sun's rays. He realizes everything around him has lines and angles. His friend Meera shows him that geometry is not just on paper—it's everywhere.

slides.title: The Discovery
slides.storyContext: Raj looks out his window and sees the edges of buildings. Meera points out that edges are really lines.
slides.inSimpleWords: Lines are straight paths that go on forever.

slides.title: What is a Line?
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a line on paper with a ruler. She explains that a line has no endpoints and goes on infinitely.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A line is a straight path with no endpoints, extending infinitely in both directions.

slides.inSimpleWords: A line never ends, it keeps going forever both ways.

image.alt: What is a Line? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Lines Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj lines in nature: a horizon line (sky meets earth), a road stretching into distance, a train track. She explains that while these look finite, in geometry they are infinite.
slides.inSimpleWords: Lines are all around us, though we see only segments of them.

slides.title: Line Segment and Ray
slides.storyContext: Raj sees the edge of his table (line segment) and the beam of sunlight (ray) coming through the window.

points.label: Line Segment
points.text: A line segment has two endpoints. Example: the edge of Raj's desk.

points.label: Ray
points.text: A ray has one starting point and extends infinitely in one direction. Example: sunlight from a window.

slides.inSimpleWords: A segment has two ends, a ray has one starting point.

image.alt: Line Segment and Ray — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Measuring Line Segments
slides.storyContext: Raj measures the edge of his table: 1.5 meters. The table leg: 0.75 meters. A pencil: 19 cm. Each is a line segment with two endpoints.

example.problem: Raj's bookshelf has 3 shelves. Each shelf is 2 meters long. If he places books along 1.5 meters of each shelf, how much empty space is there per shelf?
example.solution: Empty space = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5 meters per shelf. Total empty = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 meters. Line segment measurement applied to real objects.

slides.inSimpleWords: Line segments are the measurable parts of lines—they have length.

slides.title: What is an Angle?
slides.storyContext: Meera opens a book like a door hinge. She says the opening between the pages is an angle.

points.label: Angle
points.text: An angle is formed when two rays meet at a common point called the vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle is the space between two rays meeting at a point.

image.alt: What is an Angle? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Angles in Raj's Room
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to find angles: the corner of his desk (90°), the opening of a notebook, the corner of a door frame. Every angle has a vertex (corner) and two rays (sides).
slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are measured by how much the two rays open.

slides.title: Types of Angles
slides.storyContext: Raj measures different angles at home: the door (90°), a clock hand position (45°), and a stretched rope (180°).

example.problem: Classify these angles: 35°, 90°, 120°, 180°
example.solution: 35° is acute (less than 90°), 90° is right, 120° is obtuse (between 90° and 180°), 180° is straight.

slides.inSimpleWords: Acute angles are small, right angles are corners, obtuse are wide.

image.alt: Types of Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Classifying Angles: Complete Reference
slides.storyContext: A comprehensive guide: Acute (0-90°), Right (exactly 90°), Obtuse (90-180°), Straight (exactly 180°), Reflex (180-360°).

example.solution: 45° acute, 90° right, 120° obtuse, 180° straight, 270° reflex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every angle fits into one category based on its degree measure.

slides.title: Measuring Angles
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches Raj to use a protractor to measure the angle formed by the book pages.

points.label: Protractor
points.text: A protractor is a tool to measure angles. Place the center on the vertex and read the degree marking.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use a protractor to measure angles in degrees.

slides.title: Using a Protractor
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj step-by-step: (1) Place the center dot of the protractor on the angle's vertex. (2) Align one ray with the 0° line. (3) Read where the second ray crosses the scale. Raj practices measuring angles in his homework.
slides.inSimpleWords: A protractor is like a ruler for angles.

slides.title: Finding Angles Around You
slides.storyContext: Raj finds angles in his room: corner of floor (90°), clock showing 3:00 (90°), open notebook (varies).

example.problem: What angle does a clock hand make at 3:00 and 6:00?
example.solution: At 3:00, the angle is 90°. At 6:00, the angle is 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make different angles at different times.

image.alt: Finding Angles Around You — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Clock Angles: A Pattern
slides.storyContext: Clock hands move: hour hand (0.5° per minute), minute hand (6° per minute). At 3:00, they form 90°. At 6:00, they form 180°.

example.problem: What angle do clock hands make at 9:00?
example.solution: At 9:00, hour hand points to 9, minute hand points to 12. Angle = 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles on a clock follow a pattern—every hour is 30° apart.

slides.title: Complementary and Supplementary Angles
slides.storyContext: Two angles can relate: complementary if they add to 90°, supplementary if they add to 180°. Example: 30° and 60° are complementary.

points.label: Complementary
points.text: Two angles that sum to 90°. Example: 35° + 55° = 90°.

points.label: Supplementary
points.text: Two angles that sum to 180°. Example: 120° + 60° = 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Complementary angles 'complete' a right angle; supplementary angles 'complete' a straight line.

slides.title: Finding Missing Angles
slides.storyContext: Raj sees two angles next to each other on a line. One is 60°. What is the other if they're supplementary?

example.problem: If angle 1 is 60° and angle 1 + angle 2 = 180°, find angle 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: If two angles are supplementary and you know one, you can find the other.

slides.title: Angle Hunt
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to find and classify 5 angles in his home.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Find angles at home: door frame (90°), pencil box lid, scissors opening, window corners.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and name the angles you see.

slides.title: Vertically Opposite Angles
slides.storyContext: When two lines cross, they form 4 angles. The angles opposite each other (across the vertex) are equal. Raj draws an X and measures: both top angles are 70°, both bottom angles are 110°.

example.problem: Two lines cross. One angle is 50°. What are the other three angles?
example.solution: Opposite angle: 50°. Adjacent angles: 180° - 50° = 130° each. The four angles are 50°, 130°, 50°, 130°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite angles are equal; adjacent angles are supplementary.

slides.title: Parallel and Intersecting Lines
slides.storyContext: Railway tracks never meet (parallel). Roads at an intersection cross (intersecting). Meera draws parallel lines and shows how a line cutting both creates equal angles.

points.label: Parallel
points.text: Lines that never meet, no matter how far they extend.

points.label: Intersecting
points.text: Lines that cross at a point.

points.label: Perpendicular
points.text: Lines that intersect at 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lines can be parallel (never meet), intersecting (cross), or perpendicular (cross at right angles).

slides.title: Transversal and Angles
slides.storyContext: A transversal is a line cutting two parallel lines. Raj notices that the angles formed follow patterns: corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal. Geometry has hidden symmetries.
slides.inSimpleWords: When a line cuts two parallel lines, angles follow predictable patterns.

slides.title: Angles Made by a Transversal
slides.storyContext: Two parallel railway tracks are cut by a road (transversal). The angles formed at each track are related. If the angle at track 1 is 60°, then the corresponding angle at track 2 is also 60°.

example.problem: A transversal cuts two parallel lines. One angle is 75°. Find the other angles.
example.solution: Corresponding angle: 75°. Alternate angle: 75°. Adjacent angle: 180° - 75° = 105°. All angles are either 75° or 105°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines cut by a transversal create angles with predictable relationships.

slides.title: Challenge: Angle Construction
slides.storyContext: Draw a 45° angle using a protractor, then draw its complementary angle. Verify they sum to 90°.

points.label: Steps
points.text: Use protractor to mark 45°, then 90° - 45° = 45°. Both angles are equal (complementary).

slides.inSimpleWords: You can construct angles by understanding how they relate to 90° and 180°.

slides.title: Challenge: Real-World Angle Problems
slides.storyContext: A ladder leans against a wall, forming a 60° angle with the ground. What angle does it make with the wall?

points.label: Solution
points.text: The ladder, wall, and ground form a right angle (90°). If ladder-ground = 60°, then ladder-wall = 90° - 60° = 30°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles in triangles and real-world scenarios follow mathematical rules.

slides.title: Challenge: Spot All Angles at Home
slides.storyContext: Find 10 angles in your home, measure each with a protractor or estimate, and classify them (acute, right, obtuse, straight).

points.label: Examples
points.text: Door corners (90°), window opening (varies), corner of notebook (90°), scissors opening (acute), wall-floor angle (90°).

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are everywhere—the more you look, the more you see geometry in real life.

slides.title: Geometry in Nature
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj photos of geometry in nature: a spider's web (intersecting lines and angles), a honeycomb (perpendicular lines forming angles), a snowflake (angles and symmetry). Nature is full of geometry.
slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry isn't just on paper—it's in every natural and human-made object.

slides.title: Lines and Angles Review
slides.storyContext: Raj summarizes what he learned: lines never end, rays have one start, angles form between two rays.

points.label: Lines
points.text: Infinite straight paths with no endpoints.

points.label: Segments & Rays
points.text: Segments have two endpoints, rays have one.

points.label: Angles
points.text: Formed by two rays meeting at a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lines, segments, rays, and angles are the building blocks of geometry.

image.alt: Lines and Angles Review — Lines and Angles

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Magic Numbers
hook: Meera finds hidden patterns in numbers while organizing her school supplies.

slides.title: Meera's Magic Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera organizes her pencils, books, and erasers. She counts them, arranges them in patterns, and notices mathematical relationships. Every number has a secret: it divides, multiplies, and connects to other numbers in surprising ways.

slides.title: Numbers Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Meera counts her pencils: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. She notices every number is made of pairs.
slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers follow patterns we can discover.

slides.title: Even and Odd Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges pencils in pairs. Some pencils pair perfectly (even), one pencil is left alone (odd).

points.label: Even Numbers
points.text: Numbers divisible by 2 with no remainder: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12...

points.label: Odd Numbers
points.text: Numbers that leave remainder 1 when divided by 2: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11...

slides.inSimpleWords: Even numbers divide by 2 perfectly, odd numbers don't.

image.alt: Even and Odd Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Pairing Game
slides.storyContext: Meera lines up 10 erasers (even—pairs perfectly) and 11 erasers (odd—one left over). Raj sees the pattern: even numbers always pair; odd numbers always have one left.
slides.inSimpleWords: Even and odd is about pairing.

slides.title: Identifying Even and Odd
slides.storyContext: Meera writes numbers: 15 (ends in 5, odd), 24 (ends in 4, even), 37 (ends in 7, odd), 50 (ends in 0, even).

example.problem: Is 123 even or odd? Is 456 even or odd?
example.solution: 123 ends in 3 (odd), 456 ends in 6 (even). Last digit determines parity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look at the last digit—if it's 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, it's even; if it's 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, it's odd.

slides.title: Finding Factors
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges 12 pencils in different rectangular groups: 2×6, 3×4, 1×12.

example.problem: Find all factors of 12.
example.solution: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (numbers that divide 12 with no remainder).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factors are numbers that divide another number evenly.

slides.title: Multiples
slides.storyContext: Raj notices that if 3 is a factor, then 3, 6, 9, 12, 15... are multiples of 3.

points.label: Multiple
points.text: A multiple of a number is the result of multiplying it by any whole number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples are what you get when you skip-count.

slides.title: Skip-Counting
slides.storyContext: Meera skip-counts by 3s: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18... by 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25... Raj notices 15 appears in both—it's a common multiple.
slides.inSimpleWords: Skip-counting reveals multiples.

slides.title: Multiples and Factors Together
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: if 5 is a factor of 20, then 20 is a multiple of 5.

example.problem: List multiples of 4. Then find which numbers have 4 as a factor.
example.solution: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... Numbers with 4 as factor: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 (same list!).

slides.inSimpleWords: If X is a factor, then numbers it makes are multiples of X.

image.alt: Multiples and Factors Together — Number Play

slides.title: Prime and Composite
slides.storyContext: Meera groups numbers: some (like 2, 3, 5, 7) can only be divided by 1 and themselves (prime). Others (like 4, 6, 8, 9) have more factors (composite).

points.label: Prime
points.text: A number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.

points.label: Composite
points.text: A number with more than two factors. Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers can't be divided except by 1 and themselves.

slides.title: Finding Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj tries dividing 7 by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6—none divide evenly. Only 1 and 7 divide 7. It's prime! He tries 9: 3 × 3 = 9, so 9 is composite.
slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers are 'lonely'—only 1 and themselves divide them.

slides.title: Identifying Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj tries to divide 13 by 2, 3, 4... None work. 13 is prime!

example.problem: Is 15 prime or composite?
example.solution: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors 1, 3, 5, 15. It is composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide by small numbers; if nothing works except 1, it's prime.

slides.title: Prime Numbers Up to 20
slides.storyContext: Meera lists primes: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19. She notes 2 is the only even prime.

example.problem: Why is 2 the only even prime?
example.solution: Every even number > 2 is divisible by 2, so it has at least 3 factors (1, 2, itself). Therefore, no even number > 2 is prime.

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 is special—it's even and prime.

slides.title: Divisibility Rules
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches shortcuts: a number is divisible by 2 if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8; by 3 if digits sum to a multiple of 3; by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5.

points.label: Divisible by 2
points.text: Last digit is even.

points.label: Divisible by 3
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 3.

points.label: Divisible by 5
points.text: Ends in 0 or 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules let you check division quickly without calculating.

slides.title: Using Divisibility Rules
slides.storyContext: Is 246 divisible by 3? Sum of digits: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12. 12 is divisible by 3, so 246 is divisible by 3.

example.problem: Is 135 divisible by 3 and 5?
example.solution: Divisible by 5? Ends in 5, yes. Divisible by 3? 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, divisible by 3, yes. So 135 is divisible by both.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use divisibility rules to quickly check if numbers divide evenly.

slides.title: Number Detective
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj: find all prime numbers between 1 and 20, then find all multiples of 3.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use division rules to identify number patterns.

slides.title: Challenge: GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Meera gives Raj two numbers: 12 and 18. Find the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and Least Common Multiple (LCM).

points.label: Solution
points.text: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. GCD = 6. Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36... Multiples of 18: 18, 36... LCM = 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the biggest number that divides both; LCM is the smallest multiple of both.

slides.title: HCF (Highest Common Factor) and LCM (Least Common Multiple)
slides.storyContext: Meera has 12 red pencils and 18 blue pencils. She wants to make identical bundles with no pencils left over. What's the largest bundle size? (HCF) What's the smallest number of pencils to make equal stacks of red and blue? (LCM)

points.label: HCF
points.text: The largest number that divides two numbers evenly. For 12 and 18: HCF = 6.

points.label: LCM
points.text: The smallest number divisible by two numbers. For 12 and 18: LCM = 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: HCF finds the biggest common divisor; LCM finds the smallest common multiple.

slides.title: Finding HCF and LCM
slides.storyContext: Meera finds HCF of 20 and 30: factors of 20 (1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20), factors of 30 (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30). Common: 1, 2, 5, 10. HCF = 10. Multiples of 20: 20, 40, 60... Multiples of 30: 30, 60, 90... LCM = 60.

example.problem: Find HCF and LCM of 15 and 25.
example.solution: Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. Factors of 25: 1, 5, 25. HCF = 5. Multiples of 15: 15, 30, 45, 60, 75... Multiples of 25: 25, 50, 75... LCM = 75.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break numbers into factors and multiples to find HCF and LCM.

slides.title: Challenge: GCD and LCM Problem
slides.storyContext: Two buses depart at the same time. One runs every 12 minutes, the other every 18 minutes. When will they depart together again? (Find LCM of 12 and 18.)

points.label: Solution
points.text: LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes. They depart together again after 36 minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM solves real-world problems involving cycles and repetition.

slides.title: Challenge: Pattern Prediction
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj a sequence: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. What's the pattern? What's the next number?

points.label: Solution
points.text: Each number is multiplied by 2. Pattern: 2^n (2 to the power of n). Next: 32 × 2 = 64.

slides.inSimpleWords: Number sequences follow rules—find the rule and predict the next number.

slides.title: Playing with Squares and Cubes
slides.storyContext: Raj notices patterns: 1×1=1, 2×2=4, 3×3=9, 4×4=16... (square numbers). Then 1×1×1=1, 2×2×2=8, 3×3×3=27... (cube numbers). Meera says these are 'perfect' numbers with special properties.
slides.inSimpleWords: Square numbers result from multiplying a number by itself; cube numbers from multiplying three times.

slides.title: Square Numbers and Cube Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges pencils in a square grid: 3×3 = 9 pencils. She builds a cube: 3×3×3 = 27 pencils. She shows Raj the first 5 squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25) and cubes (1, 8, 27, 64, 125).

example.problem: Is 49 a square number? Is 64 both a square and a cube number?
example.solution: 49 = 7 × 7, yes. 64 = 8 × 8 (square) and 4 × 4 × 4 (cube), yes!

slides.inSimpleWords: Some numbers are special—they're both squares and cubes.

slides.title: Challenge: Mystery Number
slides.storyContext: Meera gives Raj clues: The number is even. It's divisible by 3. It's less than 30. It's a multiple of 4. What is it?

points.label: Solution
points.text: Multiples of 4 less than 30: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. Even (all are). Divisible by 3: 12 or 24. Both work, but most likely 12 or 24. If it's prime-like, 24. If simpler, 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use divisibility rules as clues to find mystery numbers.

slides.title: Challenge: Find All Properties
slides.storyContext: Meera gives a number: 36. Find: (a) Is it even or odd? (b) Is it prime or composite? (c) All its factors. (d) Its square root. (e) Is it a multiple of 6?
slides.inSimpleWords: A single number can have many properties; list them all to understand it deeply.

slides.title: Number Play Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj summarize: even/odd divide numbers, factors divide evenly, multiples come from skip-counting, primes are special.

points.label: Concepts
points.text: Even (÷2), Odd (÷2 with remainder), Factors (divide evenly), Multiples (skip-count).

points.label: Special Numbers
points.text: Prime (two factors), Composite (more than two factors).

slides.inSimpleWords: All numbers have patterns in how they divide and multiply.
